title: Durable Objects, Unbound
note: Head-writer outline. Words are narration targets (the film totals ~3,000 at ~140 wpm for ~24 min with holds). Each shot lists the facts it may use (claim ids), the teaching beat and the staging. Writers may split or merge lines but keep shot ids, order and claims. Illustrative fixtures (FX01): harbour room, message #42 'the ferry is late', houses A/B/C, epochs 7/8/9.

chapters.title: The Tick
chapters.summary: Cold open on one promised message. It is acknowledged; the machine that acknowledged it goes dark; another house brings the room back with the message intact. The mystery and the three promises.

shotList.purpose: Establish the harbour town (long multiplane push from the sea to House A's lit window); the Room Lantern; the sender types #42 'the ferry is late'; the slip pauses at the lantern's door; an ink tick lands. Name the fixture as made-up but the kind of room real (a chat room, the 2020 demo's own example).

Lamp change: House A's window gutters out (the process is gone). A held silence (minDuration). Up the hill House C lights; its keeper draws a bundle up from the Well and the lantern relights in C's window; the sender's slip still carries its tick. 'The machine that made that promise is gone. The promise is still true.'

Crane down to the Well and the Plate above it. The question: how did the promise outlive the promiser, and why is the answer a bucket, which cannot run a line of code? Name the stakes as two promises (one owner at a time; nothing acknowledged is ever lost) and a third, newer one: the room can move to any machine you own.

Title card over the Well: DURABLE OBJECTS, UNBOUND. One or two lines: this is a story from 2020 to the last days of October 2026, about a room, a well and a ribbon; and a promise to label what is real code and what is our made-up harbour.

chapters.title: One Room in the Whole World
chapters.summary: 2020-2024 on Cloudflare's network: one object in one place; the held reply; the open runtime that could leave but whose rooms could not travel; SQLite in the same thread and the hosted relay that made every write durable. The room was portable, but only inside Cloudflare.

shotList.purpose: 28 September 2020. Kenton Varda's desk (screen-left, warm lamp), name card. Dissolve to a paper globe with a single lantern: each object has a globally unique identifier and exists in one place in the world at a time (Q01 on screen). Requests about the same thing go to the same place, which can coordinate.
The 2020 demo was a chat app: one object per room; Q02 on screen. Our harbour room is that kind of room. Careful aside: one home does not make every step of a handler one big transaction.

3 August 2021, 'Easy, Fast, Correct — Choose three': the output gate. The Held Letter introduced: while a write is in progress, outgoing messages are held back (Q03 fragment); if the write fails the message becomes an error and the object restarts. The tick, it turns out, is a held letter released.

27 September 2022: workerd open-sourced under Apache 2.0 (Q04 short). The runtime could leave Cloudflare; the room could not travel: its Durable Objects ran as a single instance (foreshadow; the 2026 words come in ch04). 26 September 2024: SQLite inside the object, in the very same thread; local reads effectively zero latency (Q05 as fragment), but a tick is not a local read.

The hosted Storage Relay Service (badge 'Cloudflare, hosted'): it watches the write-ahead log, batches changes to object storage up to every ten seconds; object storage is slow (tens or hundreds of milliseconds), so each commit also goes to five followers in five data centres and is confirmed when three answer (Q06). First sight of the Ribbon. Close: the machinery that made a room survive a machine was real, and it lived inside Cloudflare's network.

chapters.title: The Well That Learned to Say No
chapters.summary: The bucket's dated education, a naive race with the condition pulled out, conditional create and compare and swap, the hidden referee inside the well, why 'compatible' is not a guarantee, and the one-key scope.

shotList.purpose: The Well (badge 'Amazon S3'). Before December 2020 it could hand back yesterday's copy after an overwrite (writes and reads on different cache paths, as Werner Vogels later explained). 1 December 2020: strong read-after-write consistency for all applications: the bucket you draw is the latest. Two months after Durable Objects.

PULL THE PIN (first use; the demonstrator's hand pulls the Tooth's pin). Keepers from A and B arrive at the empty Plate at once; each reads 'nobody', each writes 'mine'; both lanterns light; B's plate lands last and wins the Well; A has already served. 'An overwrite can win the well. It cannot take back what was already served.' Pin goes back.

20 August 2024: conditional create (only if absent): the shutter falls after one create, the other card refused. 25 November 2024: compare and swap on the version: both cards notched with the same old version; one click, the Plate's notch re-cut; one thunk. The store checks the condition, not the client. Term tags: compare and swap. 'The well learned to say no: three kinds of no in four years.'

WHO REFEREES THE REFEREE? Crane down into the Well cutaway. Werner Vogels name card. S3 built strong consistency from a cache coherence protocol, per-object ordering and a witness notified every time an object changes (Q17). They proved it with proofs and model checking, which took more work than the code (Q18). The machines above stop running consensus; the coordination moves inside the well.

A bucket that only looks the same: a second well, same shape, accepts both cards silently. celld (badge 'celld 0.6.3') names the stores it qualifies, warns that some compatible stores lack the conditions and that a store ignoring them fails late and silently (Q24). So every node runs four test writes, create, refuse, update, refuse-stale, plus a ranged read, before it serves.
Scope: one Plate per room; the Well referees one key at a time: no promise that two rooms change together. And if the Well goes quiet, nobody can take a Plate. Hold on the Plate, iris out.

chapters.title: Two Lineages, One Commit
chapters.summary: 2026: celld from the Deno team; Kenton Varda names workerd's gap and welcomes celld; the team joins Cloudflare with announced plans and no stated terms; the 28 October commit begins the merge.

shotList.purpose: Ryan Dahl's desk (screen-right), name card. Why he started celld (own-word label, HI13): one Rust binary whose only outside service is object storage. Released in August 2026. Self-hosted distributed Durable Objects from your existing configuration; its README says it needs no consensus service (Q19), and now we know where the consensus went. Its log replicator descends from Litestream (credit on sources card).

Kenton Varda's desk, lamp; the gap: workerd's Durable Objects ran as one instance only (own-word label, HI12); Kenton's welcome (Q10 fragment). The two desk lamps in one frame; two ropes begin to braid.

9 October 2026: the entire Deno team joining Cloudflare (Q12 fragment). Announced plans, said plainly as plans: the runtime supported for one more year, then development ends (HI16, own words); Deploy six months; JSR continues on Cloudflare; rusty_v8 continues; Deno remains open source. Neither post states a price or terms. Ryan Dahl and Bert Belder (name card) to lead first-class workerd self-hosting, bringing celld's code and ideas into workerd (HI18, own-word label).

28 October 2026, Pacific time: the commit, as a parchment strip of its own message: Q14; several processes, one shared bucket, one owner per object, takeover from the bucket; experimental; no ack until the bucket holds the write (own-word label, HI21); Q16. Two days later, alarms; the next day, facets. Badges `workerd · 28 Oct` and `workerd · 31 Oct` hung for the rest of the film. 'Let us open it.'

chapters.title: The Plate and the Candle
chapters.summary: workerd's ownership record and leases: the Plate's three tiles, the Candle's arithmetic, a scar in a comment, the self-fence pin, borrowed clocks (and celld's different rule), and claimed versus opened epochs.

shotList.purpose: The Plate up close: house · epoch · from, the only authority for who owns the room and whose log holds its latest commits. A claim is a compare and swap: a free plate or one naming a house whose lease ran out is taken with the next epoch; exactly one claimant wins. A brand new room is created already open in one conditional write; the loser is pointed at the winner. Routes are a remembered direction, not proof (refreshed at most every five seconds).

Paper-fold into the Candle ruler. Lease twenty seconds; renew every three; each attempt allowed four; a clock may be two seconds off the bucket's; the painted band is twice that, four seconds. With an expiry at twenty thousand milliseconds, serve only while your clock reads under sixteen thousand; start a renewal only under twelve thousand. Boundaries, not promises about timers. Term: lease.

Why four seconds and not two: a comment in the code records that R2 stalls writes about five and a half seconds at every five-minute mark, and a two-second bound once fenced every node. A real scar, kept in the code. Failed renewals retry while the lease still covers the attempt.

PULL THE PIN (self-fence). A's keeper falls asleep at the window (a paused process); the candle burns into the band; B finds A's lease expired and takes the Plate; A wakes and serves on: two rooms. Pin back: before it renews, A checks whether it would still hold four seconds ahead; it would not; it closes its own shutters; the lamp goes out: the process exits. 'A timeout proves silence. It does not prove death.' The rule treats an unrenewed house as gone; safety comes from the old owner stopping itself in time, and from a second look we will meet in the ribbon. Term: fencing.

Borrowed clocks: each house measures its skew against the bucket's clock, and when it cannot measure it assumes zero. An assumption, so not the last line of defence. celld (badge) does it differently: ten-second leases renewed after a third, and its acknowledgement check consults the record, not a clock (LE12, own-word label).

CLAIMED IS NOT OPENED. The Plate tiles step: A·7·from 7 (crown lit). B claims: B·8·from 7 (crown unlit). B restores, uploads its starting snapshot, and only then opens: from becomes 8. Suppose B dies before opening: C claims C·9·from 7 and recovers seven's log, because eight never opened and acknowledged nothing. Rewind: had B opened, B·8·from 8, and C would recover eight. 'The difference decides which past the room comes back with.' Term: epoch.

chapters.title: The Ribbon
chapters.summary: SQLite's write-ahead log as a ribbon; cutting whole transactions; scrolls, books and checksums in the well (workerd's own format; celld's LTX is different); proof before response; the re-read pin; a lost reply proves nothing.

shotList.purpose: Inside the Room Lantern: SQLite in the same thread; the main file and, beside it, the write-ahead log, a ribbon. Leader of thirty-two bytes; each frame a twenty-four-byte tab and one page; on the last frame of a transaction a seal carrying the database's size after the commit. That number is the commit mark. Term: write-ahead log.

The keeper's Scissors: the runtime watches every write SQLite makes to the log, buffers frames since the last seal, and cuts only when a seal completes: one whole transaction. A transaction that rolls back is simply written over by the next one. When SQLite starts the log afresh after a checkpoint, the keeper starts a fresh ribbon.

Down the line to the Well: frames merged to the newest version of each page, rolled into scrolls labelled by session and end, tied with a gzip cord whose knot records a checksum and length, so a damaged scroll refuses to be read rather than reading wrong. Each epoch starts its own session with a Book (snapshot) of what it inherited; when scrolls pile up to the size of the room a new Book is bound, uploaded before the old scrolls are cleared. Badge: this is workerd's own format; celld writes a different one, LTX.

PROOF BEFORE RESPONSE. The Held Letter with #42's reply. Cut the transaction; scroll down the Well; then the keeper's lamp lifts to the Plate one more time; still A·7; the bell; the latch lifts; the tick. Many letters share one walk to the Well, and each is released when the bell covers its own place on the ribbon. In workerd, local completion is not the tick; the bucket is. celld lists everything its gate holds: replies, errors, even each chunk of a stream (Q25).

PULL THE PIN (the second look). A wakes after B has claimed epoch 8; its scroll lands in session 7; without the second look A rings the bell, a tick for a write B will never restore. Pin back: A's lamp lifts, the Plate says 8, no bell; the letter becomes an error; A's late scroll is left for the next epoch to clear. Coda: a lost reply proves nothing either way (DU08): durability is not exactly-once.

chapters.title: The Neighbours
chapters.summary: C rebuilds the room from the Well; every tick paid for a trip to the Well; celld's fleet presses the tail into neighbours' notebooks; the tail now lives outside the Well; the recovery gate seals and collects it; a complete tail is required, and without one the room stays shut.

shotList.purpose: C's takeover (workerd): wipe the local copy; read the newest Book, then each scroll in order, skipping pages already applied; a missing scroll in between stops the restore cold; a checksum can say a scroll is damaged, never what it said; pages are replayed, nobody's code is re-run. #42 returns.

The price: every tick waited for a trip to the Well and a look at the Plate (widths illustrative, not measured). Cloudflare's hosted relay used followers; celld (badge) does too. Lamp change to celld's town, labGreen windows.

The Neighbours: the owner hands each committed page to one or two neighbouring copyists; each must turn their book press (fsync) before the bell rings; the tick can come before the Well. The owner never counts itself, so a fleet needs two running houses; with two neighbours, three copies; with only one, a fresh write lives in two places until the Well catches up; with none, back to the Well, slower but correct. Term: fsync.

The new danger. The owner dies with acknowledged pages only in neighbours' notebooks. PULL THE PIN (no seal): epoch prefixes keep a stale owner's scrolls out of the current lineage in the Well, but they cannot recover what only the neighbours hold: #42 would vanish, or a stale owner could still collect another bell. So before its first such tick, each celld session writes a conditional record of its log.

THE RECOVERY GATE (parchment, numbered steps). Before the successor reads the Well, it reads the predecessor's log record. Absent: it never ticked past the Well. Sealed: already recovered. Open: compare and swap to fence it; seal the reachable neighbours' notebooks with wax; collect their retained pages; upload them; mark the record sealed; only then restore (CE06, CE07; own-word label).

A COMPLETE TAIL. At least one current neighbour must hand over its complete retained range. Illustrative case one: neighbour one's notebook is water-damaged, neighbour two's is complete: recovery proceeds. Case two: one incomplete, one damaged: no complete proof; the door stays shut. An error from a neighbour is no evidence its pages are gone (CE09, own-word label). 'The room would rather stay shut than come back missing a promise.'
Houses restarting together can still lend each other their notebooks; recovery can take minutes and keeps retrying. The lantern relights; #42 still has its tick.

chapters.title: What Travels
chapters.summary: The contract assembled; what the operator must do; dated limits; the announced direction attributed; the tick as a proof.

shotList.purpose: PIN MONTAGE: every pin we pulled, in one slow pan: the Tooth, the band, the second look, the seal. What travels when a room travels is not the bucket alone: it is the bucket's one-key refusals and fresh reads, a supervisor to restart a house that fenced itself, and a runtime that cuts, uploads, looks again, seals and replays. Remove any one and a pin falls.

The small print, dated 31 October 2026. workerd's clustering began behind an experimental flag with no alarms; by the thirty-first it had alarms and facets; its tests check single-writer state, forwarding and takeover; we read them, we did not run them; an alarm test is not exactly-once. celld wants a supervisor and a bucket whose lifecycle rules leave its records alone, and documents its own limits. workerd on its own is not a sandbox for untrusted code.

The two desk lamps once more: the announced direction, in their own terms, a first-class way to run this yourself, with celld's ideas merged in. What the Well will never do: run your code, change two rooms at once, promise exactly once, or stay up for you.

Dawn over the harbour. The lantern in House C's window; the sender's slip with its tick. 'A tick is not a feeling. It is a proof': the bytes were in the Well, and the Plate still named its owner when the bell rang. Pull back to the whole town. End card with the three pins (versions) and 'illustrative harbour; real code'.
